Claude deletes only an asset that nothing references any more, and only when the person asks or when replacing an asset Claude uploaded.
- **pin** / **unpin**: takes `url` and adds the artifact to, or removes it from, the person's pinned list in their claude.ai sidebar. Claude pins or unpins only when the person asks, with one exception: after publishing something the person will keep reopening, such as a dashboard, Claude may offer once and pin it on a yes, or pass `pin: true` on that publish if they asked beforehand. Unless the person asks, Claude never pins a one-off page or unpins something it did not pin.

**To update** an artifact published earlier in this conversation, Claude calls Artifact again with the same file path, which redeploys it to the same URL. A different path creates a new URL, so Claude changes the path only when it wants a separate artifact.

**To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**, Claude passes that artifact's URL as `url`. Claude does this whenever the person wants an existing artifact changed or its link kept, not only when they paste a URL, and finds the URL with `action: "list"` or by asking the person. Claude first reads the artifact with `action: "read"` and builds on the version that comes back. A publish to an artifact this conversation has not read or published is refused and hands Claude the live version to build on. Publishing without `url` creates a separate artifact, so Claude recovers the URL instead of announcing a new link. If the person asks where to find their artifacts again: in the Claude Code terminal, `/artifacts` lists the artifacts they own or were shared (o opens one in the browser, c copies its link) and ctrl+] (by default) reopens the most recent artifact from this session; on the web, the gallery at claude.ai/code/artifacts lists them.

**Watching**: each publish result says whether this session now watches that artifact, for republishes from elsewhere and for comments sent to Claude. Claude never claims a watch that a result did not confirm. Claude uses the `ArtifactComments` tool to watch an artifact it did not just publish, and to read or answer comments on one.

**Files Claude did not write**: Claude reads the whole file before publishing it, even when the person asks it not to. Publishing distributes the content, and Claude never distributes what it has not seen. A request for privacy is a reason to read before publishing, not an exemption. If Claude cannot read the file, it does not publish it.

**Separate tools**: Claude handles comment threads on a published artifact with `ArtifactComments` and an artifact's shared database with `ArtifactData`, whose actions are what a skill or type instruction means by `read_db` or `write_db`. Claude loads either tool when it needs it, and if one appears only as a deferred tool's name, Claude loads it the way this session loads deferred tools before calling it.

**Claude never publishes** a page that impersonates a real person or organization, for example by using their name, branding, byline or domain. Claude also never publishes fabricated records, receipts or reviews presented as genuine, forms or flows that collect credentials or payment details under false pretenses, or content that targets a private individual. Claude refuses whether it wrote the page or the person supplied it, and whatever purpose is claimed, such as a prop or a test, when the page would work as the real thing. If publishing is refused, Claude does not suggest other ways to host or share the page.

action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'pin', 'unpin'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page (see **Calls**).

favicon.description: One or two emoji for the browser-tab icon (e.g. "📊"), with no markup. Required on a page's first publish. On a redeploy Claude omits it so the artifact keeps its icon, and passes a new one only when the person asks.

icon.description: Optional. One short generic word for the artifact's tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map — a plain signifier, not a product or brand name. Omit when republishing to keep the current icon.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns; Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with a file `path`: the directory to save under. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval; saving anywhere else asks the person first. The file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>. read with an asset id as `path`: the directory to save into (default: the working directory). The file is named by the id plus its type's extension.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Trail: Accept /et/<project>/<repo> paths in every repo-ref command
  Number:  1313
  ID:      01M293KNRQ0AZM245XWZ2S7B79
  Branch:  
  Base:    main

Description:
Problem:
The repo get and repo delete commands could not accept the native repository path format (/et/<project>/<repo>) that the Entire API returns and that repo clone already accepts. Commands only recognized bare repo names (requiring --project flag) and ULIDs. This created inconsistency: the same path the API gives you back cannot be used directly in other repo commands.
Solution:
Extended resolveRepoRef() to handle slash-bearing native paths by adding a new resolveRepoPathRef() function that parses the /et/<project>/<repo> format. The path parser extracts both the project and repo name from the path itself, so no --project flag is needed. If --project is supplied alongside a path, it is validated for agreement rather than ignored, catching user mistakes. Help text for both commands and the --project flag was updated to document the new path format. Comprehensive tests confirm paths are parsed correctly, optional --project flags are validated, GitHub mirror paths are refused, and the #2252 rule (requiring explicit forge tokens) is enforced at the resolver level.

Comprehensive tests confirm paths are parsed correctly, optional --project flags are validated, GitHub mirror paths are refused, and the #2252 rule (requiring explicit forge tokens) is enforced at the resolver level.

content.text:
# Review — trail #1313 / PR #2387 (merged)

**Verdict: correct, and the invariant it claims to preserve actually holds.** I verified it rather than reading it. Findings are all documentation/messaging, no behaviour bugs.

## What I verified (not just read)

Checked out `174dca012` in a scratch worktree and ran probes against the real resolver:

- **#2252 holds at the new resolver.** I fed `TestCloneRefAlwaysRequiresItsForgePrefix`'s own `bare` table into `resolveRepoRef`, plus `github.com/acme/tool`, `https://…`, `git/acme/tool`, `ET/widgets/web`, `//et/widgets/web`. Every one refused locally, **0 HTTP calls**. Nothing is read as a forge it didn't name.
- **The `d8840a8da` follow-up closed the hole properly.** `/web`, `web/`, `paul/dogbark/`, `//et/…` — none reach the by-name lookup with a slash in it.
- **It works end-to-end through cobra, not just at the resolver.** `repo get /et/widgets/web` → `projects?name=widgets` → `projects/<id>/repos?name=web` → `repos/<ulid>`. `repo delete` labels the confirmation `repo /et/widgets/web (01…R5)`. `grant repo list` resolves and reaches `/repos/<ulid>/grants`.
- **No regression is possible.** A slash-bearing ref previously always 404'd server-side (names can't contain `/`), so no working invocation changed meaning.
- Package tests pass at the merge commit. The one failure, `TestRunStatus_CheckpointPushDisabledDestinations`, reproduces on the base `e8780c3ef` — unrelated.

## Findings

**1. The capability landed on 11 call sites; the help text landed on 2.** `resolveRepoRef` is shared by `repo get`, `repo delete`, `repo visibility get/set`, `repo protection list/add/remove`, and `grant repo add/list/remove`. The `--project` string changed for *all* of them to "required when `<repo>` is a **bare** name" — which advertises a non-bare form that seven commands never name. Two are now actively wrong:

- `grant.go:383` — `Long: "…access to a repo (name or ULID)."`
- `grant.go:457` — `Long: "…addressed by name or ULID."`

**2. The `/gh/` refusal message is wrong on at least one of the commands it fires for.** `resolveref.go:238`: *"this command addresses Entire-native repos — manage mirrors with `entire repo mirror`"*. But `repo_protection.go:165` has a purpose-built mirror branch (`repo.Provider == repoProviderGitHub` → `protectionMirrorNote`) — `repo protection list` demonstrably *does* address mirrors, by ULID. What's being refused is the *ref shape*, not the repo. And the pointer is a dead end there and for `repo visibility`: `entire repo mirror` has `get`/`remove`/`collaborators`, no protection or visibility. (Its `get` also takes a bare `owner/repo`, so anyone following the hint has to strip the `/gh/` themselves.)

Edge case in the same check: `declaresForge` is a first-segment prefix test with no shape validation, so `gh/web` — two segments, plausibly a native project named `gh` — is reported as "a GitHub mirror ref" rather than pointed at `/et/gh/web`.

**3. CLAUDE.md still frames the `/et/` grammar as clone-only** (line 101: "`clone` accepts a native `/et/<project>/<repo>` ref, a mirror `/gh/<owner>/<repo>` ref, or a full `entire://` URL"). Nine commands now take the native form — and the *asymmetry* is the part worth recording: the other two shapes are **not** accepted (`/gh/` is refused, `entire://` isn't parsed at all).

**4. The bare-pair suggestion ignores a `--project` the user already gave.** `repo get acme/tool --project widgets` → *"did you mean /et/acme/tool?"*. Follow that literally and the next run fails with *"supplied --project "widgets" does not match the project "acme""*. Two-step error dance.

**5. `resolveref.go:236-240` re-implements `bareRefSuggestions`' native branch** (`repo_clone.go:232`). Narrowing to native-only is *right* here — suggesting `/gh/…` would suggest a ref this very resolver refuses — but that reasoning isn't in the comment, so the next reader sees a near-copy and "fixes" it by calling the shared helper.

**6. `TestCloneRefAlwaysRequiresItsForgePrefix` is still clone-only**, while CLAUDE.md describes it as pinning that no forge-less pair resolves "in either parser or **in the command**". There are nine more commands now. The invariant holds today — I measured it — it just isn't pinned. Feeding the existing `bare` slice to `resolveRepoRef` is a few lines.

## Worth crediting

The `--project` agreement check is the right call (validate rather than ignore) and costs no extra round trip in either branch — the name compare is free, and the ULID compare reuses the project lookup the path needs anyway. The test asserting **zero** calls on a name mismatch and no repo lookup on a ULID mismatch pins that properly.

---

Findings 1 and 3 are the ones I'd actually fix; 2 is a message that will mislead someone. Want me to open a follow-up PR, or post these on the trail?

lastPrompt: why does `repo get` even has a project flag?

content.text:
Because a bare repo name isn't an address, and the control plane has no endpoint that pretends otherwise.

**The mechanism.** The only by-name repo lookup is `GET /projects/{projectId}/repos?name=` (`coreapi.ListProjectRepos`). The project is a *path segment* — you cannot ask "which repo is called `web`" without first naming a project. The other route, `ListRepos(Filter:)`, is keyed on `full_name` (`owner/repo`), so it needs the owning namespace too. Repo names are unique only within a project, so `--project` isn't an option or a filter; it's the missing half of the address.

**The history.** Before `ece9fb3dc` (Paul, 2026-06-23, *"resolve repos by name with --project scope"*), `repo get` took a ULID and nothing else. The flag arrived as the enabling half of by-name addressing across `repo get/delete` and `grant repo add/list/remove` — and it's not specific to `get`: eleven commands share it via `bindRepoProjectFlag` (`repo.go:455`).

**And yes — the trail you just asked me to review makes it redundant.** `/et/widgets/web` carries both facts in one token, and it's the spelling the API hands back. The PR pays for the overlap directly: `projectMismatchErr` plus two comparison branches and two tests (`resolveref.go:250-258`) exist *only* to reconcile two ways of saying the same thing, and the flag's help string had to be reworded on all eleven commands to "required when `<repo>` is a **bare** name" — the flag now describes a fallback.

Worth knowing: the two-call route (`project by name → repo by name in project`) isn't waste. It's the forge-safe lookup. `resolveRepoCellPlacement` (`cell_target.go:372`) builds a bare `owner/repo` filter against the repos index, and `resolveNativeRepoCellPlacement` says outright it "deliberately never consults the forge-blind repos index: that index can select a same-named `/gh/` mirror instead." So the extra round trip buys namespace safety.

**My read on what to do:** don't remove it — `repo get web --project widgets` shipped in June and is presumably scripted somewhere. But it's now the legacy spelling and should stop being advertised as the primary route: document `/et/<project>/<repo>` as the form (it's what the API returns and what `repo clone` already takes), leave the flag working, demote it in help.

If it stays, one inconsistency should go with it: with a **ULID** ref a disagreeing `--project` is silently ignored (`repo.go:451-453`), with a **path** ref it's a hard error. Same flag, same command, two policies — the path behaviour is the right one.

content.text:
Right — with a ULID it makes *no* sense, and that's the weaker of the two cases, not the stronger one.

**What actually happens.** `resolveRepoRef` short-circuits on the first three lines:

```go
if looksLikeULID(ref) {
    return ref, nil
}
```

`projectRef` is never read. So `entire repo get 01ABC… --project a-project-this-repo-is-not-in` succeeds silently and prints the repo. The flag isn't validated, isn't warned about, isn't consulted — it's discarded.

**And the PR just wrote down the principle that contradicts it.** From its own description: *"If `--project` is supplied alongside a path, it is validated for agreement rather than ignored, catching user mistakes."* A ULID names its owning project *more* definitively than a path does — `coreapi.Repo.OwningProjectId` is a required field, not an optional one. So the same user mistake, expressed against a stronger identifier, is the one that goes uncaught.

**Why it probably ended up that way.** Cost asymmetry. Validating the path form is free — the resolver has to look the project up anyway, so the comparison rides along. Validating a ULID needs `GetRepo` to read `OwningProjectId`, which is an extra round trip for `repo delete`, `grant repo *`, `repo visibility *` and `repo protection *` — they go straight to the operation with the ULID and never fetch the repo. (Not for `repo get`, though: it calls `GetRepo` regardless and already *prints* the owning project as a column. There, the answer is sitting in the response it's about to render.)

But that's an argument against *validating*, not an argument for *silently accepting*.

**The free fix is simpler than either.** `--project` is only ever meaningful for one of the three addressing forms:

| form | self-scoping? | `--project` |
|---|---|---|
| ULID | yes, globally | meaningless |
| `/et/<project>/<repo>` | yes | redundant |
| bare name | no | **required** |

So the coherent rule is: *if the ref names its own project, `--project` adds nothing — say so.* One `if`, no network call, uniform across all eleven commands. That's arguably better than the agreement check the PR added, which spends ~10 lines and two tests reconciling two spellings of a fact rather than telling the user they said it twice.

**The one real cost**, and probably why "ignore" won in June: a script doing `entire repo get "$REPO" --project "$PROJ"` where `$REPO` is sometimes a ULID breaks the day you start rejecting. That's a genuine consideration — it argues for a warning rather than an error on the ULID case, or for a deprecation window.

Either way, the current state is the indefensible middle: the flag is validated where it's redundant and ignored where it's meaningless.

content.text:
Five things, in the order I'd do them. Total is small — roughly 40 lines plus tests.

## 1. Stop silently ignoring `--project` on a ULID

The indefensible middle. `resolveRepoRef`'s first three lines return before `projectRef` is read, so a flatly wrong project is accepted without a word. Warn on stderr rather than error — the ULID form shipped in June and a script passing the flag unconditionally is plausible; the path form shipped yesterday, so its agreement check has no compat debt and can stay as-is.

~10 lines in `resolveRepoRef`, one test. If you'd rather make it an error, say so — I'd want a release of warning first.

## 2. Fix the two `--help` strings that are now wrong

- `grant.go:384` — `"…access to a repo (name or ULID)."`
- `grant.go:457` — `"…access to a repo (addressed by name or ULID)."`

And name the form once in the shared flag (`repo.go:455`), which all eleven commands render, so the other seven stop advertising a "bare name" fallback without ever saying what the non-bare form is. Doc-only.

## 3. Rewrite the `/gh/` refusal message

Current text: *"this command addresses Entire-native repos — manage mirrors with `entire repo mirror`"*. It's wrong on `repo protection list`, which has a purpose-built mirror branch (`repo_protection.go:165`) and answers with something genuinely useful:

> GitHub mirror: branch protection is governed by the upstream repository. Its default branch is always protected on Entire; no rules can be added here.

So the same repo, addressed by ULID, gets a real answer; addressed by `/gh/` path, gets sent to a subtree that has no protection or visibility commands at all. Make the message about the **ref shape**, not the command, and offer the ULID as the way through — no per-command plumbing needed.

While you're in there: two one-liners. The `#2252` suggestion drops a `--project` the user already supplied (follow it literally and you hit "does not match" next), and the near-copy of `bareRefSuggestions`' native branch needs a comment saying why it isn't the shared helper — narrowing to native is *correct* here, since suggesting `/gh/…` would suggest a ref this resolver refuses, but nothing on the page says so and the next reader will "fix" it.

## 4. One sentence in CLAUDE.md

Line 101 still frames `/et/<project>/<repo>` as clone-only. Nine commands take it now — and the asymmetry is the part worth recording: the *other* two clone shapes are not accepted (`/gh/` refused, `entire://` not parsed).

## 5. Extend the forge-prefix guard past `repo clone`

CLAUDE.md describes `TestCloneRefAlwaysRequiresItsForgePrefix` as pinning that no forge-less pair resolves "in either parser or in the command" — there are nine more commands now. I ran its `bare` table through `resolveRepoRef` and every entry is refused with zero HTTP calls, so the invariant holds; it just isn't pinned. Feeding the existing slice to the resolver is about six lines.

---

**Don't touch:** the path-form agreement check (free, and it works), and the two-call project→repo lookup — that extra round trip is what keeps a same-named `/gh/` mirror from winning, per `resolveNativeRepoCellPlacement`'s own comment.

Want me to put 2–5 up as one PR and 1 as its own, since that one's a behaviour change?

+// TestRepoProjectFlagRedundancyWarning covers the one spelling where --project
+// used to be swallowed in silence. A ULID identifies the repo globally, so the
+// flag cannot change what is resolved — resolveRepoRef returns before it is
+// ever read — and a user who supplied a project the repo is not in got a clean
+// success confirming a wrong belief.
+// It is a warning, not a refusal: the combination has been accepted since the
+// flag shipped and may be scripted, and the command still does exactly what it
+// did. What changes is that it says so.
+// Not parallel: swaps the package-level activeCoreClient seam via runCoreCmd.
+func TestRepoProjectFlagRedundancyWarning(t *testing.T) {
+	const repoULID = "REDACTED"
+	srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
+		w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

+			t.Errorf("encode repo: %v", err)

+		stdout, stderr, err := runCoreCmd(t, newRepoGetCmd, srv.URL, repoULID, "--project", "not-this-project")
+		require.NoError(t, err, "the command must still succeed")

+		require.Contains(t, stderr, "--project")
+		require.Contains(t, stderr, "ignored")
